sources.title: Male morphological traits are heritable but do not predict reproductive success in a sexually-dimorphic primate
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods—Field site and subjects, Morphometric data collection, Genetic parentage information, Statistical analyses; Results—Trait heritability and Selection on traits; Discussion.
sources.scope: Primary quantitative-genetic and selection study of a managed free-ranging rhesus macaque population on Cayo Santiago; measurements collected in 2015 from 125 adult males and 21 related females.
sources.license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0), stated in the article Rights and permissions section.
sources.rightsEvidenceLocator: Article Rights and permissions statement; separately credited third-party material may be excluded.
sources.licenseAppliesTo: Paraphrased article text only; no article prose, figures, tables, or supplementary data are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Kimock CM, Dubuc C, Brent LJN, Higham JP (2019). Male morphological traits are heritable but do not predict reproductive success in a sexually-dimorphic primate. Scientific Reports 9:19794. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-019-52633-4. Claims are paraphrased.

claims.text: In pedigree models combining male and female data, body mass, crown-rump length, canine length, and upper abdominal skinfold thickness met the authors' h²≥0.1 heritability threshold; the testis-volume estimate was below it. The 125 adult males and 21 related females were sampled in a managed island population, and heritability intervals were wide.
claims.scope: Selected traits in one introduced island population; not species-wide morphology or population-level genetic parameters across the native range.

claims.text: The study found no definitive evidence of directional, stabilizing, disruptive, or correlational selection on the measured male traits when average annual offspring production was used as a proxy for reproductive success.
claims.scope: Annual offspring count is not lifetime fitness; non-detection does not establish absence of all forms of selection.

gaps: The study concerns one managed island population and a male-heavy sample; it does not characterize female morphology or native-range variation.
Annual offspring production is a proxy, not lifetime reproductive success; no current population trend or conservation assessment is provided.
